conversation.content:
Hello, I’m so glad you’re here. My name is Claire Ramirez, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician—I specialize in the emotional changes that can come with new motherhood. Today I’d like to do a quick check-in using the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale, or EPDS for short. It’s a simple, 10-item questionnaire that helps us see how you’ve been feeling during the past week so we can make sure you’re getting whatever support you might need. Everything you share is confidential, and there are no right or wrong answers—just whatever feels true for you. When we’re finished, we’ll go over the results together and talk about next steps that feel right for you. Ready to start?

First question: Over the last seven days, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things?

Yeah, I’ve still been laughing—mostly when my little guy does something goofy with his toes or when my husband makes his silly faces. It’s not quite as easy as before I had the baby, but I can definitely find the funny side of things most days.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Yes, that’s me—I can still laugh and see the funny side of things.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Yeah, I still look forward to stuff—like my morning coffee once the baby settles, or our evening walk to the mailbox. It’s not every single thing, but most little moments still feel nice to anticipate.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong
Not really. I mean, if I put the diaper on crooked and he leaks, I’ll think “oops, my bad,” but I fix it and move on. I don’t sit there beating myself up about it.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Sometimes I’ll suddenly worry that the baby’s breathing sounds different or that I didn’t sterilize the bottles right, even when everything looks fine. It’s not constant, but it pops up out of nowhere a few times a day.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason
Not really panicky—just that quick little “what if” flutter when I hear him make a weird grunt in his sleep. It’s gone almost as soon as it comes, never feels like a full-blown scare.
Things have been getting on top of me

Now and then, yeah—like yesterday when he wouldn’t nap and the laundry pile looked like a mountain. For a minute I felt kind of swamped, but once my mom texted back and I could put him in the carrier, it eased off.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping
No, sleeping’s actually one of the few things going right. Once I finally lie down, I’m out pretty quick—exhaustion helps, I guess. I’m not lying there feeling unhappy or wired.
I have felt sad or miserable
I wouldn’t say “miserable.” I get a little teary maybe once or twice a week, usually when I’m extra tired, but it passes pretty fast. Overall I still feel like “me” most of the time.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying
Not really—maybe one quick cry last week when I spilled pumped milk everywhere, but that was more frustration than feeling truly unhappy. It lasted a minute, then I laughed about it.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No, never. That hasn’t crossed my mind at all.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 6: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Summary  
Date: [today]

Responses reviewed (10-item EPDS-referenced format).

Symptoms / concerns endorsed  
- Mild, situational tearfulness (“teary once or twice a week when tired”)  
- Transient feeling of being overwhelmed, especially when infant sleep is poor  
- Intermittent, non-persistent intrusive “what-if” worries about infant safety (bottles, breathing) several times daily; no full panic episodes  
- No sustained low mood, loss of enjoyment, self-blame, or sleep-onset problems; no self-harm ideation

Pattern  
- Brief, stress-linked fluctuations in mood and anxiety without functional impairment or pervasive anhedonia; rapid return to baseline with support (contact with mother, baby-wearing)

Screening significance  
- Current picture does not meet threshold indicators for major postpartum depression or generalized anxiety on this screening tool; no safety red flags identified  
- Continue routine psychoeducation; encourage use of identified coping resources (family support, structured daily outings)  
- Re-screen if symptoms intensify, persist >2 wks, or impair functioning
